title: The Serge Country to the Bond Market: Baring, the Commutation Act, and the Money for Louisiana
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Serge Country and the Seven Years

stops.name: Larkbeare near Exeter, the birth in the wool merchant's house
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Place unresolved: the sources say only Larkbeare, near Exeter, and two houses of that name compete, one a farmstead in the parish of Talaton eleven miles north-east, one on the southern edge of Exeter itself. The Exeter city pin is used as an honest fallback; the coordinate 50.781/-3.369 carried in earlier working notes matches neither candidate and is not published here.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of April a son is born to Johann Baring, a wool merchant out of Bremen who took English naturalization and with it an English name, John, and to Elizabeth Vowler, whose family money underwrites the serge business he has built. Exeter at this hour is one of the great cloth-exporting cities of England, shipping its worsteds to Holland and Germany and Spain. He is given the name Francis. The house is called Larkbeare, and the record does not agree with itself about which Larkbeare.
suggested_refs: Larkbeare Road, Exeter EX2, and the Larkbeare hamlet in Talaton parish, the two rival sitings of the birth
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Exeter, the father dead and the widow at the books
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: John Baring dies at fifty-one and leaves a wool-exporting house at the top of the Exeter boom, three sons, a daughter, and no arrangement for a manager. Francis is eight years old and will be apprenticed in London seven years from now. Elizabeth Vowler Baring takes the business into her own hands and keeps it through the whole of her sons' minority. The capital that will one day underwrite bond issues in Amsterdam and Paris sits for those years in a widow's ledgers in a provincial cloth town.
suggested_refs: The Exeter serge trade of the 1740s, in which the Baring capital was first accumulated
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Hoxton, the French school north of the City
stops.date_confidence: The two schools are attested; the year is not. Sources date the schooling only to the early 1750s, and 1751 is used here purely to order the segment. Coordinate corrected to Hoxton proper, 51.5324/-0.0783, from an earlier working value that fell some five hundred metres away on the Shoreditch side.
stops.campa: The boy is sent up from Devon and put into Mr Fargue's French school at Hoxton, then a village of academies on the fields north-east of the City, where merchants' sons are taught the language they will need for correspondence with Rouen and Amsterdam. He will not go to a university. His schooling is chosen for a career already decided, and it is chosen by a mother running a business she means her sons to inherit intact. The sources give the school and the master's name and not the year.
suggested_refs: Hoxton's eighteenth-century private academies, the schooling merchants bought instead of a university

stops.name: Lothbury, the academy of accounts
stops.date_confidence: Attested as the second school; the year is an ordering device only, the sources giving no date beyond the early 1750s.
stops.campa: From Hoxton he moves to Mr Fuller's academy in Lothbury, a lane running behind the site where the Bank of England will raise its blank wall. The curriculum is bookkeeping, commercial arithmetic, the forms of a bill of exchange, the drafting of a letter that will hold up in a foreign court. There is no Latin in it. These academies sell a counting house exactly what it asks for and nothing beyond it. Francis Baring is thirteen, and this is the end of his formal education.
suggested_refs: Lothbury, City of London, and the commercial academies serving the counting houses around it

stops.name: The City of London, apprenticed to Samuel Touchet
stops.date_confidence: Year and terms attested; the exact address of Touchet's countinghouse was not located, and a general City pin is used.
stops.campa: At fifteen he is bound apprentice for seven years to Samuel Touchet, a Manchester cotton manufacturer turned London merchant and Member of Parliament, for a premium reported at eight hundred pounds. Touchet's business runs to the Levant, to West Africa, and to the West Indies; it deals in fustians, in colonial produce, in insurance, and in slaving voyages. Bills, freights, insurance, the pricing of a risk at four thousand miles: Francis Baring learns all of it here. He is at this desk until he is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: Samuel Touchet's London mercantile and West India business, in which Baring served his indentures
sources: Madge Dresser and Andrew Hann, The Slavery Connections of Northington Grange (Historic England, 2013)

stops.name: Touchet's countinghouse, the year the Lydia clears for Africa
stops.date_confidence: The Lydia's slaving voyage under Touchet is attested to 1757, which corrects the 1756 date and the accompanying age of sixteen that circulate with the legend; Baring was seventeen and an indentured clerk. Baring's own participation is [R] and disputed: it rests on tradition, and the study that tested it could not be opened.
stops.campa: A ship of Touchet's, the Lydia, sails on a slaving voyage; another, the Favourite, will follow four years later. Out of this proximity grows the story, repeated for two centuries and still repeated, that Francis Baring made his first fortune in the slave trade at sixteen. Historic England's archival study of the Baring slavery connections went looking for his name in the ownership records of the voyages, did not find it, and judged investment by an apprenticed clerk extremely unlikely. He was seventeen, not sixteen, and he was indentured.
suggested_refs: Madge Dresser and Andrew Hann, The Slavery Connections of Northington Grange (English Heritage/Historic England, 2013), which tested and rejected the claim; Peter Fryer, Staying Power (1984), named as the modern origin of its circulation
sources: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (negative result for Baring)

stops.name: London, the articles signed on Christmas Day
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The seven years end on Christmas Day, and the three Baring brothers sign articles the same day founding two linked houses: John & Francis Baring & Co. in London, John & Charles Baring & Co. in Exeter. John is the elder and the senior name; Charles keeps the Devon wool business their father built; Francis, twenty-two, is to run London. For the next fifteen years the two houses will share partners and share liability. The indentures end and the partnership begins on the same winter day.
suggested_refs: The 1762 articles of partnership founding the linked London and Exeter houses

stops.name: Cheapside, John & Francis Baring & Co. opens for business
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged, not resolved. Working notes gave the opening as 1 January 1763 at Mincing Lane; the firm's own history says the house started in offices off Cheapside and moved to Mincing Lane within a few years, and dates the founding to 1762. The Cheapside siting is used here and the precise opening date is unsourced, carried only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The house opens in offices off Cheapside with a capital of some ten thousand pounds and a partner who is silent by preference. John Baring lends the name and the money and stays out of the day; Francis takes the desk. What they are is not yet a bank. They are merchants. They buy and sell goods on their own account and on other people's, take commissions, accept bills, insure cargoes, and lend against all of it. The firm's own history dates the founding to 1762 and the move to Mincing Lane to within a few years of this.
suggested_refs: The Cheapside offices of John & Francis Baring & Co., the firm's first address

stops.name: Croydon, the marriage at St John the Baptist
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Francis marries Harriet Herring, daughter of the London merchant William Herring, in the parish church of Croydon, ten miles south of the City where both their fathers did business. They will have twelve children, ten of whom reach adulthood. It is a merchant's marriage into a merchant family, the first of a run of them: his sons will marry into Philadelphia the same way. Under the floor of this church lies Thomas Herring, sometime Archbishop of Canterbury, a relative of the bride.
suggested_refs: Croydon Minster, formerly St John the Baptist, and the tomb of Archbishop Thomas Herring

stops.name: Mincing Lane, the house above the countinghouse
stops.date_confidence: The move from Cheapside to Mincing Lane is attested to within a few years of 1763; the month here orders the segment against the marriage. The street number 6, which appears in working notes, is corroborated by nothing fetched and is not asserted.
stops.campa: The firm moves down to Mincing Lane, a short street of brokers and merchants sloping toward the Thames wharves, and Francis and Harriet take the rooms above it. For twenty-three years the family lives on top of the business, and there is no distinction yet between a Baring and the Baring house, because there is nowhere for one to stand. Clerks come up the stairs with letters from Amsterdam and Philadelphia; the children learn the sound of a ship's manifest being read aloud; the counting house and the nursery share a chimney.
suggested_refs: Mincing Lane, City of London, the firm's second address and the family's home to about 1790
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: The Royal Exchange, the court of the Assurance and the underwriting room
stops.date_confidence: The court appointment of 1771, held to 1780, is attested. The underwriting at Lloyd's is ODNB-derived; Lloyd's occupancy of the Royal Exchange is independently attested, the individual risks Baring took are not itemized in any source consulted.
stops.campa: At thirty-one he is appointed to the court of the Royal Exchange Assurance and holds the place for nine years. The Exchange is a trapezoidal courtyard at the meeting of Cornhill and Threadneedle Street where the merchants of London stand in assigned walks by nation and trade, and Lloyd's underwriters take marine risks in rooms inside the same building. Baring underwrites there too. Which cargoes and which hulls he put his name to is not itemized in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: The Royal Exchange, Cornhill, housing both the Royal Exchange Assurance and Lloyd's underwriting room

stops.name: Mincing Lane, the first account in North America
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The house opens its first North American correspondent account, one year before Lexington. The colonies are about to stop being colonies, and the men whose names will fill the Baring ledgers for the next forty years are already in place: Thomas Willing and Robert Morris in Philadelphia, and Morris's young partner William Bingham, whose daughters two of Baring's sons will marry and a million acres of whose Maine land the house will one day buy. Then the war comes, and the letters stop.
suggested_refs: The Willing & Morris correspondence, opening of the Baring house's American network

stops.name: Exeter, the brother's speculations and the partnerships dissolved
stops.date_confidence: The dissolution of the interlocking partnerships in 1777 is attested. The two quoted phrases survive in the Baring Archive and are quoted in Orbell's ODNB life; no primary letter was opened here.
stops.campa: Charles Baring, holding the Exeter house their father founded, has been speculating, and Francis reads the accounts. He describes his brother's dealings as speculations of a wild, strange, incoherent description, and calls the whole business an almost monstrous management of the original and chief dependence of the Baring family. The interlocking partnerships are dissolved in 1777. Charles keeps Exeter and the wool trade that made the family. Francis takes London and the capital.
stops.quote: of a wild, strange, incoherent description
stops.quote_source: Francis Baring on his brother Charles's Exeter speculations; Baring Archive, Northbrook MSS D1, quoted in John Orbell, ODNB
suggested_refs: Baring Archive, Northbrook MSS D1 and D7, the family correspondence on the Exeter house
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

segments.name: Leadenhall Street and the Prince of Merchants

stops.name: East India House, elected to the Court of Directors
stops.date_confidence: The directorship from 1779 to his death is attested through the ODNB-derived account and the Company's director lists; the month is not given in any source consulted.
stops.campa: He is elected a director of the East India Company and will hold a seat, with the statutory breaks the charter requires, until the year he dies: thirty-one years of it. The Court sits at Leadenhall Street in a house whose Palladian front hides a warren of committee rooms where a chartered corporation governs provinces and keeps an army. Baring is thirty-nine, a merchant with no landed name, and he has been put there by the Company's own proprietors. He will chair it once, thirteen years from now.
suggested_refs: East India House, Leadenhall Street, seat of the Court of Directors

stops.name: Bowood, the confidential adviser to Lord Shelburne
stops.date_confidence: The advisory relationship, beginning when Shelburne became prime minister in July 1782, is attested. Baring's physical presence at Bowood is not: no source consulted places him there, and the visit is traditional. The sobriquet Prince of Merchants reaches us at one remove only.
stops.campa: William Petty, Earl of Shelburne, becomes prime minister and takes as his confidential commercial adviser a merchant with no rank and no party, to be consulted on the peace with America and on what trade between the two countries should look like once one of them is no longer the other's possession. At Bowood, Shelburne keeps Priestley in the house and reformers at the table, and Baring is drawn into that circle. Shelburne is said to have called him the Prince of Merchants. Whether Baring ever came down to Wiltshire, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: Bowood House, Wiltshire, and the Shelburne circle of the 1780s
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: East India House, against Fox's India Bill
stops.date_confidence: The opposition to the North and Fox India proposals is attested. The quoted sentence is a manuscript utterance in the Baring Archive, quoted in Orbell's ODNB life; it appears in no printed pamphlet or parliamentary text and must not be cited as a speech.
stops.campa: Lord North and Charles James Fox move to put the Company's Indian government under a board of commissioners named by Parliament, and the City rises against it. Baring is among the loudest. His objection is not only about patronage or about the Company's charter, and he puts it in a sentence written in his own hand: India is not a colony and God forbid that it ever should be. The bill passes the Commons and dies in the Lords. The ministry falls with it, and Pitt takes office in December.
stops.quote: India is not a colony and God forbid that it ever should be
stops.quote_source: Francis Baring on the North and Fox India proposals; Baring Archive, Northbrook MSS N4.5, quoted in John Orbell, ODNB
suggested_refs: Baring Archive, Northbrook MSS N4.5; the East India Bill of 1783 and its defeat in the Lords
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Grampound, the borough bought for three thousand pounds
stops.date_confidence: The return for Grampound in 1784, at a reported cost of about £3,000, is attested; the month is the general date of the 1784 general election. Whether Baring ever went to Cornwall, as against buying the seat through agents, is not established by any source consulted. History of Parliament Online returned HTTP 401.
stops.campa: Grampound is a decayed town on the River Fal with a few dozen electors and a reputation, even by the standards of Cornwall, for selling itself without embarrassment. Baring takes the seat for something like three thousand pounds and holds it six years. He is forty-four and has wanted Parliament for a while, not for office, which he never seeks, but because the questions he cares about, the tea duty and the Company charter and the currency, are settled in a room he has until now had to lobby from outside.
suggested_refs: The borough of Grampound, Cornwall, disenfranchised for corruption in 1821

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster, the deaf member on finance
stops.date_confidence: The parliamentary career from 1784 to 1806 across four Parliaments is attested; the assessment of his speaking manner is ODNB-derived and impressionistic.
stops.campa: He takes his seat and sits, across four Parliaments and twenty-two years, for Grampound, then Chipping Wycombe, then Calne, then Chipping Wycombe again. He is going deaf, which makes the cut and thrust of debate nearly impossible, and he never becomes an orator. He asks for no office and is given none. He is forty-four when he first sits and sixty-six when he stops. What contemporaries record instead is a man who rises on a finance question, states the figures, states what follows from them, and sits down.
suggested_refs: The History of Parliament, House of Commons 1790-1820, on Baring's speaking record
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Mincing Lane, the pamphlet on the Commutation Act
stops.date_confidence: The pamphlet is attested and its text verified from the second edition, London: J. Sewell, 1786, on the Internet Archive. Earlier working notes cited a third edition; the digitized copy states the second on its title page. The month is unrecorded.
stops.campa: Pitt has cut the duty on tea from around one hundred and twenty per cent to twelve and a half, gambling that a cheap legal leaf will kill the smuggling trade outright, and the gamble is attacked from every quarter. Baring answers with figures. His pamphlet sets the old revenue against the new, prints the balance, and concludes that the Publick purchase their Tea for £2,055,462 less than was formerly paid by them. He signs nothing. He refers to himself throughout, in the third person, as the Author.
stops.quote: The Author of these Sheets writes neither from party views, nor upon party principles.
stops.quote_source: Francis Baring, The Principle of the Commutation-Act Established by Facts, 2nd edn (London: J. Sewell, 1786), p. 5
suggested_refs: Internet Archive item principleofcommu00bariuoft, the 1786 second edition, full text and page images
sources: Francis Baring, The Principle of the Commutation-Act Established by Facts, 2nd edn (1786)

stops.name: Keizersgracht, the cochineal corner with Hope & Co.
stops.date_confidence: The operation and its loss are attested. Baring's own presence in Amsterdam is not: the corner was run through agents and through the Hope house, and no source consulted places him in the city. The pin is Hope & Co.'s house at Keizersgracht 444-446, correcting an earlier working value that pointed at the Dam.
stops.campa: With Hope & Co. of Amsterdam, Baring sets out to corner the European supply of cochineal, the Mexican insect dye that colours every red coat in Europe. Correspondents from Cadiz to St Petersburg spend some four hundred and fifty thousand pounds buying it up. The price does not rise. It sits, and by 1788 the partners have renounced a whole year's profit share to absorb what the operation has cost them. Baring himself never goes to Amsterdam. The whole thing is run by letter.
suggested_refs: Hope & Co., Keizersgracht 444-446, Amsterdam, the Baring house's principal continental ally
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Ilchester, the seat lost
stops.date_confidence: Unverified. The 1790 Ilchester contest and defeat rest on the ODNB-derived account alone; Wikipedia's Ilchester article records nothing of it and History of Parliament Online returned HTTP 401. Carried as attributed, not as established. Coordinate corrected to the village centre.
stops.campa: Out at Grampound and looking for a seat, he contests the Somerset borough of Ilchester at the general election and loses it. Ilchester is another of the small corrupt boroughs of the west country, and it declines to be bought by him. In a career where money and Lansdowne's interest almost always deliver a constituency, this is the one clean failure on the parliamentary record, and even it is thinly attested: no printed account of the contest could be located, and it survives on the authority of a single biographical entry. He is out of the Commons for four years.
suggested_refs: The History of Parliament, House of Commons 1790-1820, entry for Ilchester
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

segments.name: The Chair, the Baronetcy, the Bank

stops.name: East India House, the chairman's year
stops.date_confidence: The chairmanship for the 1792-93 term and the charter negotiation are attested. The quoted sentence is from a letter in the Baring Archive, quoted in Orbell's ODNB life; the manuscript itself was not opened here. The month sets the start of the Company year.
stops.campa: He is elected chairman of the East India Company in the year the charter falls due for renewal, with Parliament, the ministry, and the Company's own directors all pulling different ways. He negotiates the 1793 renewal, and it takes the whole of his term. To Lord Lansdowne he writes the sentence that is the whole of his opinion of the men he is chairing: the more I work, the greater the degree of jealousy and difficulty I have to encounter amongst the directors who are in general composed of either knaves or fools.
stops.quote: The more I work, the greater the degree of jealousy and difficulty I have to encounter amongst the directors who are in general composed of either knaves or fools.
stops.quote_source: Francis Baring to Lord Lansdowne, during the 1792-93 East India Company chairmanship; Baring Archive DEP193.17.1, quoted in John Orbell, ODNB
suggested_refs: Baring Archive DEP193.17.1; the East India Company charter renewal of 1793
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the house outgrows Mincing Lane
stops.date_confidence: The relocation to Devonshire Square in 1793, on account of expanded business, is attested; the month is not. The street number 11 appears in working notes and is corroborated by nothing fetched, so the square is carried without a number.
stops.campa: The business has outgrown the sloping lane by the wharves, and the firm moves north to Devonshire Square near Bishopsgate, a square of merchants' houses with room for a growing establishment of clerks. Thirty years after the Cheapside room, the Baring house accepts bills for correspondents on four continents and has begun the business it will be remembered for, which is lending to governments. Britain declares war on France in February of the same year, and the firm's government business dates from about here.
suggested_refs: Devonshire Square, City of London, the firm's address from 1793

stops.name: Westminster, created a baronet
stops.date_confidence: Date of creation attested. That the honour was recognition of his East India Company service and the charter negotiation is the conventional reading and is not stated in any patent text consulted.
stops.campa: Pitt's government creates him a baronet, four days short of a year into the chairmanship and with the charter business barely settled. The Devon wool merchant's son, apprenticed at fifteen with no university and no land, is now Sir Francis Baring, and the title is heritable. Nothing in the letters patent says why; that it paid for the charter negotiation is the conventional reading and is nowhere written down. The patent styles him of Larkbeare, the house near Exeter that nobody has since been able to place.
suggested_refs: The baronetcy of Baring of Larkbeare, created 29 May 1793

stops.name: Chipping Wycombe, the Lansdowne boroughs
stops.date_confidence: The constituencies and their dates are attested: Chipping Wycombe 1794-96 and 1802-06, Calne 1796-1802. The month is an ordering device. Personal presence in either borough is undocumented.
stops.campa: He returns to the Commons for Chipping Wycombe, a borough under Lansdowne's control, and afterwards for Calne, which sits a few miles from Bowood's park wall. The political partnership begun with Shelburne in 1782 has outlasted Shelburne's ministry by a dozen years and now runs through his son. Baring never holds office and never asks for any. He holds a seat, which is a different instrument. Chipping Wycombe 1794 to 1796, Calne 1796 to 1802, Chipping Wycombe again 1802 to 1806.
suggested_refs: The Lansdowne parliamentary interest at Chipping Wycombe and Calne

stops.name: Devonshire Square, eight hundred thousand dollars for the Barbary states
stops.date_confidence: Reported, not verified. The figure of up to $800,000 of United States six-percent stock marketed for the Barbary negotiations, with funds advanced ahead of the sale, is corroborated only in general outline; no primary document was opened. Carried as [R].
stops.campa: The United States needs to buy peace from the deys and beys of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, whose corsairs are holding American crews for ransom, and it has no money in Europe to buy it with. Barings undertakes to sell up to eight hundred thousand dollars of American six-percent stock in London, and advances the funds before the stock is placed. The house is now carrying the cash flow of a foreign republic. The figure is reported rather than documented; no contract for it was opened here.
suggested_refs: Baring Archive records of United States government business, 1795-1804
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the son sent to America
stops.date_confidence: The mission and the purchase are attested; the purchase is dated late 1795 and the price given as £107,000 for over a million acres. The lower bound of £90,500 and the date of early 1796 that circulate in working notes are unsupported. The month here orders the departure against the purchase. Alexander travelled; Francis did not, so the stop stands at the London desk that authorized it.
stops.campa: Francis sends his nineteen-year-old son Alexander across the Atlantic to look at William Bingham's Maine lands and report. Alexander looks, and instead of reporting buys: over a million acres of the District of Maine for Barings and Hope & Co., for a hundred and seven thousand pounds, before the year is out. He had authority to inspect and not to purchase. Francis does not recall him. He extends the credit and lets him stay, and the son will not come home for three years.
suggested_refs: The Bingham Purchase lands in the District of Maine, bought for Barings and Hope & Co. in late 1795

stops.name: Manor House, Lee, the country seat within reach of the City
stops.date_confidence: Purchase in 1796 for £20,000 attested; the month is not recorded. The vendor was Mrs Angerstein, formerly Mrs Lucas, correcting an account that had the sale run through Joseph Paice as trustee for Thomas Lucas, who was the estate's 1770s developer. Coordinate corrected to the Manor House and its grounds in Manor Lane.
stops.campa: He buys the Manor House at Lee near Blackheath from Mrs Angerstein, who was formerly Mrs Lucas. It is a Georgian box in its own grounds, close enough to the City that a man can sleep out of it and be at his desk in the morning. He is fifty-six and has lived over the shop for thirty-three years. This is the first house he has owned that is not also an office. The price is twenty thousand pounds flat, the wider range of twenty to twenty-seven thousand that circulates elsewhere being unsupported.
suggested_refs: Manor House Gardens, Lee, where the house survives as a public library and its grounds as a park; sold by Thomas Baring, 1st Earl of Northbrook, to the London County Council in 1898 for £8,835

stops.name: The Bank of England, the day cash payments stop
stops.date_confidence: The suspension of cash payments and Baring's pamphlets answering it are attested; the quotation is verified against the page images of Further Observations, printed p. 16. Two readings that circulate in working notes are corrected there: the original has was, not were, and the public, not the Nation, the latter being an artifact of the archive's OCR truncating the line.
stops.campa: The Bank suspends payment in coin. Its notes remain, and a country at war discovers overnight that its money is paper backed by nothing but confidence in an institution William Paterson chartered a hundred and three years before. Baring writes two pamphlets in the same year defending what has been done and refusing to soften the word for it: the Bank was not insolvent, they had more than failed, and had passed beyond the line of bankruptcy. One surviving copy of the second is inscribed to Jeremy Bentham.
stops.quote: The Bank was not insolvent, they had more than failed, and had passed beyond the line of bankruptcy
stops.quote_source: Sir Francis Baring, Further Observations on the Establishment of the Bank of England, and on the Paper Circulation of the Country (London, 1797), printed p. 16
suggested_refs: Internet Archive item bim_eighteenth-century_further-observations-on-_baring-francis-sir_1797, the copy inscribed To Jeremy Bentham
sources: Sir Francis Baring, Observations on the Establishment of the Bank of England (1797)

stops.name: The Bank of England, the answer to Walter Boyd
stops.date_confidence: The pamphlet is attested and its text verified from the Internet Archive copy; the month of publication is not recorded in the source consulted.
stops.campa: Walter Boyd, a member of Parliament and a ruined banker, publishes an argument that the Bank's own note issue is what has raised prices, and Baring answers him in print at sixty. His defence is not technical. It is a claim about what the Bank is: to the agriculture, commerce, and finance of Great Britain, its sun. Along the way he sets down the sentence that explains half his career of pamphleteering, which is that the ignorant, and more particularly the half-informed, are too much disposed to place confidence in a name.
stops.quote: The Bank of England is, to the Agriculture, Commerce, and Finance of Great Britain, its sun
stops.quote_source: Sir Francis Baring, Observations on the Publication of Walter Boyd, Esq., M.P. (London, 1801)
suggested_refs: Internet Archive item observationsonpu00bariuoft, full text of the 1801 pamphlet
sources: Sir Francis Baring, Observations on the Publication of Walter Boyd, Esq., M.P. (1801)

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the Philadelphia marriages
stops.date_confidence: Alexander's marriage to Ann Louisa Bingham is attested to 1798 and Henry's to her sister Maria Matilda to 1802; only the years are given in the sources consulted. Both weddings took place in the United States, where Francis was not, so the stop stands at his own desk in London.
stops.campa: Word comes from Philadelphia that Alexander has married Ann Louisa Bingham, daughter of the American whose Maine acreage he bought. Four years later Henry marries her sister Maria Matilda. Two Baring sons, two Bingham daughters, and a Philadelphia fortune tied by marriage to a counting house in Bishopsgate. Whether Francis arranged any of it, or was told after the fact as he was told about Maine, the sources consulted do not say. Both weddings happen in America; he is at his desk in London for both.
suggested_refs: The Bingham family of Philadelphia and its alliance with the Baring house

stops.name: Devonshire Square, John Baring retires and the name changes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of April the elder brother, silent partner for thirty-seven years, retires, and the house is restyled Francis Baring & Co. John put up the money in 1762 and let his younger brother run it; he has drawn his share for a working lifetime without ever taking the desk. The name over the door now belongs to one man. That man is sixty, going deaf, and has just finished defending the national currency in print against a member of Parliament.
suggested_refs: The restyling of the London house as Francis Baring & Co., 1 April 1800

stops.name: Hill Street, Mayfair, the house in the West End
stops.date_confidence: The move to Hill Street near Berkeley Square in 1802 is attested; the month is not recorded.
stops.campa: He takes a house on Hill Street, off Berkeley Square, and the family's London address stops being in the City altogether. Mincing Lane, then Devonshire Square, now Mayfair, where the neighbours are peers of the realm and the houses have no counting rooms in them. Devonshire Square stays on as the business address and Stratton is a year old. He is sixty-two, a baronet and a Member of Parliament, and two years short of withdrawing from the trade that paid for the house.
suggested_refs: Hill Street, Mayfair, the Baring family's West End residence from 1802

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the credit that buys Louisiana
stops.date_confidence: The contract, the tranche of $11.25 million in United States six-percent bonds, and the conclusion of negotiations in Paris at the end of April 1803 are attested. The negotiating was done in Paris by Alexander Baring and Pierre Cesar Labouchere of Hope & Co.; Francis did not travel, and the stop therefore stands at the London house whose authorization and credit stood behind them.
stops.campa: In Paris, Alexander Baring and Pierre Cesar Labouchere of Hope & Co. agree to buy and distribute eleven and a quarter million dollars of United States six-percent bonds, the paper with which Thomas Jefferson's government will pay Napoleon for Louisiana. The authorization and the credit are Francis Baring's, given from a square in Bishopsgate by a house whose own country is at war with France. Britain lets it proceed. Francis is sixty-three and does not leave London; the negotiation ends in Paris at the end of April.
suggested_refs: The Baring Archive's Louisiana Purchase exhibition, drawing on letters of Francis Baring, Alexander Baring, and Pierre Cesar Labouchere
sources: The Baring Archive, 'The Louisiana Purchase' online exhibition

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the house becomes Baring Brothers & Co.
stops.date_confidence: The renaming to Baring Brothers & Co. in 1804, on the entry of Thomas, Alexander, and Henry as partners, is attested, as is the retention of that name until 1890. Working notes dating the change to 1806 and naming two entering sons are wrong on both counts; the 1806 move to 8 Bishopsgate is a separate event. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Three sons come in as partners, Thomas, Alexander, and Henry, and the house is restyled Baring Brothers & Co. It will keep that name for eighty-six years. Francis began surrendering his profit share the year before; he now retires from active partnership, leaves some seventy thousand pounds of his capital in the business, and permits his name to keep appearing on public loan contracts. The move to 8 Bishopsgate is two years off and is a separate matter, often confused with this one.
suggested_refs: The partnership deeds of 1804 constituting Baring Brothers & Co.; the firm's move to 8 Bishopsgate in 1806

stops.name: Devonshire Square, the last forty million francs
stops.date_confidence: The transfers are attested: ten million francs to France in July 1803, a further 40.35 million in April 1804 discharging the obligation. The transfers were executed on the continent by the Baring and Hope agents, not by Francis in person; the stop stands at the authorizing house.
stops.campa: Ten million francs went to the French treasury in the summer; now a further forty and a third million follow, and the obligation under the bond contract is discharged. Napoleon has been paid, in cash, by two merchant houses of a nation he is at war with, for a territory neither of them will ever see. The bonds are sold on across Europe to investors who want American paper at six per cent. The transfers themselves are made on the continent by the Baring and Hope agents; Francis Baring authorizes them from a room in Bishopsgate at sixty-four.
suggested_refs: The Baring and Hope transfers of 1803-04 discharging the Louisiana bond contract

stops.name: Stratton Park, the estate bought from the Russell heirs
stops.date_confidence: The 1801 purchase from the Russell heirs is firm and the hedged window of 1800 to 1802 in working notes is dropped. The figure of £150,000 is not a purchase price: it is the cumulative Stratton expenditure reaching that sum by 1803. The month is not recorded.
stops.campa: He buys Stratton Park in Hampshire from the heirs of the Duke of Bedford, a great chalk-country estate with a village, a church, and thousands of acres of downland. He is sixty-one and has never owned land on this scale. By 1803 he will have laid out a hundred and fifty thousand pounds on it altogether, which is cumulative spending and not a purchase price; what he actually paid for the land is not recorded in anything consulted. The Barings will hold Stratton for one hundred and sixty-two years.
suggested_refs: Stratton Park, East Stratton, Hampshire, the Baring seat from 1801 to 1963

stops.name: Stratton Park, Dance's portico and Repton's ground
stops.date_confidence: Dance's remodelling is dated 1803-06 and Repton's landscaping from about 1803; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: George Dance the Younger is set to remodel the house and puts across its front a stone Doric portico of unfluted columns, austere and archaeological, in the Greek manner just then arriving in England. Sir Francis is buying the newest architecture in the country, and no record consulted has him ever travelling outside England to see any of the buildings it copies. Humphry Repton takes the park in hand at the same time and lays out the grounds. The work runs from 1803 to 1806.
suggested_refs: The Stratton Park portico, all that survives of Dance's house after the 1963 demolition by John Baring, 7th Baron Ashburton; listed 1983, the park registered Grade II in 1984

stops.name: The Royal Exchange, the chair of Lloyd's Patriotic Fund
stops.date_confidence: The chairmanship from the Fund's founding in 1803 until his death is attested through the ODNB-derived account; the exact date is the Fund's own founding day at Lloyd's.
stops.campa: In the invasion year, with the country expecting French troops on the Kentish beaches, the subscribers at Lloyd's establish a fund for wounded servicemen and for the widows and children of the dead. It is founded at Lloyd's Coffee House on the twentieth of July, and Baring, sixty-three years old and a man of that room since his thirties, takes the chair. He holds it until he dies. Downstairs the underwriters go on writing marine risks against the same war.
suggested_refs: Lloyd's Patriotic Fund, founded at Lloyd's Coffee House, 20 July 1803
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: Bath, the death of Harriet
stops.date_confidence: The date and place of Harriet Baring's death are ODNB-derived. Whether Francis was at Bath is not established by any source consulted; the stop marks where she died. His remembered words about her reach us at one remove and are not quoted here as verbatim text.
stops.campa: Harriet Baring dies at Bath, thirty-seven years married, having borne twelve children and buried two of them small. She had come to him from a merchant's house at Croydon in 1767 and kept a household on top of a counting house in Mincing Lane for twenty-three years afterwards. Francis writes of her later as a woman of superior mind and an affectionate heart. Whether he was in the room, or in Hampshire, or at his desk in Bishopsgate when the news reached him, the record does not say. He does not remarry.
suggested_refs: The Baring family correspondence on Harriet Baring, Baring Archive
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'

stops.name: 8 Old Jewry, the London Institution
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged, not resolved. The biographical account gives Baring the presidency from 1805 until his death; the Institution itself was established on 18 January 1806, taking premises at 8 Old Jewry at £350 a year, with a royal charter drafted by January 1807. 1805 is at best a subscription or committee year. The pin is Old Jewry, not the Coleman Street and Finsbury Circus buildings the body moved to in 1812 and 1815, both after his death.
stops.campa: The merchants and bankers of the City subscribe to found an institution for science and useful knowledge in their own quarter, a library and lecture room for men who were never sent to Oxford, and they put Baring in the president's chair. He holds it until he dies. The premises are rooms at 8 Old Jewry at three hundred and fifty pounds a year, taken on the eighteenth of January, with a royal charter drafted inside the year. Whether he was in the chair from 1805, as one life has it, or only from the founding, nobody has settled.
suggested_refs: The London Institution, established 18 January 1806 at 8 Old Jewry

stops.name: Stratton Park, Lawrence paints the three partners
stops.date_confidence: The commission is attested to 1806; the month is not recorded and is set here only to order the segment. A separate attribution of a single-figure Lawrence portrait of Baring to Bowood House could not be corroborated and is not carried.
stops.campa: Thomas Lawrence is summoned down to Hampshire to paint Sir Francis with his brother John and his son-in-law Charles Wall, the three partners together, in the year the firm moves to Bishopsgate. Baring leans in toward the paper on the table with his hand cupped behind his ear, because by now he can hear almost nothing, and Lawrence paints the deafness rather than hiding it. Two years earlier Benjamin West had set him at a window with the Stratton grounds behind him, stern and upright and quite still.
suggested_refs: Thomas Lawrence, Sir Francis Baring with John Baring and Charles Wall (1806); Benjamin West, portrait of Sir Francis Baring (1804), Baring Archive, 'Baring Portraits' exhibition
sources: The Baring Archive, 'Baring Portraits' online exhibition

stops.name: The Palace of Westminster, the Bullion Committee
stops.date_confidence: Reported, not verified. The testimony before the Bullion Committee on the high price of gold rests on the ODNB-derived account and on Hidy; no primary transcript was opened. The month is the Committee's sitting period. The Fouche peace approaches reaching Baring through his son-in-law Labouchere rest on the same secondary basis and are equally unverified.
stops.campa: Gold has risen against the paper the Bank has been issuing since 1797, and Parliament appoints a committee to find out why. Baring is called and gives evidence, seventy years old and almost entirely deaf, on the question he has been arguing in print since he was fifty-seven. It is the last public act of his career. In the same year, through his son-in-law Labouchere, he is drawn at the edges into Fouche's unofficial and abortive soundings for a peace between France and Britain.
suggested_refs: The Report of the Select Committee on the High Price of Gold Bullion, 1810
sources: John Orbell, ODNB, 'Baring, Sir Francis, first baronet'
Ralph W. Hidy, The House of Baring in American Trade and Finance

stops.name: Manor House, Lee, the death
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction flagged, not resolved. Most modern biographical sources give 11 September 1810 at Lee, Kent; the historic Hansard person index gives 12 September. The Gentleman's Magazine obituary gives his age as seventy-four, which does not agree with a birth date of 18 April 1740; he was seventy. Coordinate corrected to the Manor House site in Manor Lane.
stops.campa: He dies at the Manor House at Lee, the first house he ever owned that was not also a place of business, seventy years old and fifty-five years from the day he was bound apprentice. His estate is valued at some six hundred and six thousand pounds and includes a collection of Dutch and Flemish old masters. Hansard's index says the twelfth of September; everybody else says the eleventh, and nobody has reconciled them. The Gentleman's Magazine prints an unsigned obituary that month and gives the verdict of the City in a single line, without qualifying it.
stops.quote: At his death, he was unquestionably the first merchant in Europe; first in knowledge and talents, and first in character and opulence.
stops.quote_source: Obituary of Sir Francis Baring, Gentleman's Magazine, vol. 80 part 2 (September 1810), p. 293; the phrase is often attributed to Lord Erskine, but that attribution is the Dictionary of National Biography's, and Erskine is not named in the magazine
suggested_refs: Internet Archive item sim_gentlemans-magazine_1810-09_80, obituary at p. 293

stops.name: St Mary the Virgin, Micheldever, the family vault
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Nine days after his death he is carried to St Mary the Virgin at Micheldever, the parish church nearest Stratton, and laid in the family vault. The date is the twentieth of September. The vault is nine years old and the Baring dead will fill it for two centuries. What he leaves is a bank with correspondents on three continents and a name over its door that his sons keep. Sixty-two years earlier his mother kept a dead man's books in Exeter so that her sons would have something to inherit.
suggested_refs: The Baring family vault at St Mary the Virgin, Micheldever; the Baring Archive, Northbrook Papers, 8-10 Moorgate, London, holding the unpublished correspondence
sources: The Baring Archive, 'Northbrook Papers - Business Papers'
